967.title: Exchanging self and other
967.hook: Shantideva: put yourself in another's place, completely
967.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, exchanging self and other is taught from the eighth chapter of Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara, and it underlies mind-training practices in which practitioners imagine taking on others' suffering and giving away their own happiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lazy monk. Shantideva, written off by everyone, recited the Way of the Bodhisattva. Your line: the lazy one spoke.

A stubbed toe. The hand goes straight down to it. Nobody tells the hand to, and it never stops to ask what the foot has done for it lately. It just goes, because hand and foot belong to one body. In the masterpiece the lazy monk recited, the guide to the bodhisattva's way of life, a chapter on meditation takes that ordinary reflex and pushes it as far as it will go. What if the line around the body were drawn somewhere else?
screen: `THE HAND GOES TO THE FOOT.` → `ONE BODY.` → `WHAT IF THE LINE MOVED?`

segments.voice: Shantideva builds it in steps. I want to be happy and I don't want to suffer. So does everyone else, in exactly the same way. If that's true, he asks, what makes my pain the one worth guarding? Only habit. He uses the picture of the body: the hand protects the foot as part of itself, and so beings can be cared for as parts of one life. Then the exchange itself. Put yourself where the other person stands, and look back. In one passage he has the practitioner take the place of someone worse off, then an equal, then someone better off, and look back at their old self from each seat, calling that old self he. From the other side of the table, my own pride looks very different. Why bother? Shantideva is blunt: the misery in the world comes from wanting happiness only for oneself, and the joy in the world comes from wishing others well. He calls this exchange a supreme secret, a practice for those who want to protect themselves and others quickly. And what it isn't. It isn't erasing yourself, or pretending you have no needs. The practitioner still eats and sleeps. It's a shift of where the center sits, practiced on purpose, the way a musician practices scales. Tibetan teachers later built whole trainings on this chapter. In these verses his tone is plain and urgent, with nothing sentimental in it.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS THE SAME THING.` · `STAND THERE AND LOOK BACK.` · `A SUPREME SECRET.` · `NOT ERASING YOURSELF.` · then, large: `EXCHANGE SELF AND OTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you saw yesterday, anyone at all, and sit where they sat: their chair, their morning, their tiredness, what they were hoping for. From there, look across at yourself without judging what you see, then come home to your own breath.
Exchange. Shantideva's practice of standing where another stands and wanting their good as if it were your own, which he calls a supreme secret. Today's word.
Your line: exchange self and other. The hand never asks what the foot has done for it. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

968.title: A lamp for the path
968.hook: Atisha's short text sets out the stages of the path
968.carry: has the aim grown its wings
968.howItsDone: Atisha's Lamp for the Path to Awakening is studied in Tibetan monasteries and retreat centers, and its outline of three kinds of practitioner shapes the lamrim, the stages-of-the-path teachings given in Tibetan Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shantideva's exchange, standing where another stands and looking back. Your line: exchange self and other.

A hiker at the edge of a dark trail doesn't need the whole mountain lit up. A small lamp will do, if it shows the next few steps and roughly where they lead. Atisha, the Indian teacher whose coming to Tibet brought a renewal, was asked by a Tibetan ruler, tradition says, for something simple: not a library, but a guide a person could carry. What Atisha wrote is short, and its title says what it's for.
screen: `A SMALL LAMP, A DARK TRAIL.` → `NOT A LIBRARY.` → `A GUIDE YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: It's the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. We met its outline when Atisha first came to Tibet; today, a closer look inside. The opening verses sort readers not by school but by aim. Some seek good things for themselves within the round of lives. Some turn from that round toward their own peace. And some want to end the suffering of others as if it were their own. The Lamp says plainly that the rest is written for that third person. It asks them to take refuge and raise the wish to awaken for everyone's sake, the same wish we heard from Shantideva, and then to keep vows. A wish with no conduct behind it stays a wish. For meditation, Atisha uses a plain picture: a bird whose wings haven't grown can't fly. Without a settled, steady mind, he says, a person can't do much good for others. So calm comes first. Near the end, the Lamp says that wisdom without skillful means is bondage, and skillful means without wisdom is bondage too, so keep both. Insight with no kindness binds; kindness with no insight binds another way. Later Tibetan teachers wrote whole books on this outline, a genre called lamrim, the stages of the path. The Lamp itself is short enough to carry, which was the point.
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, THREE AIMS.` · `A WISH, THEN VOWS.` · `A BIRD WITHOUT WINGS CAN'T FLY.` · `WISDOM AND MEANS, BOTH.` · then, large: `A LAMP FOR THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly, with a breath between each question: what do I want for my own life this year, what would real peace look like underneath that, and what would I wish for the people around me, all of them? Let one answer come for each, in your own words, then rest in the breath.
Lamrim. The stages of the path, the genre Atisha's short text for Tibetan practice gave rise to, sorting the path by aim. Today's word.
Your line: has the aim grown its wings. A small lamp, a few steps, and the great aim still ahead. Go gently.

969.title: Atisha's cook
969.hook: a legend: Atisha kept a bad-tempered cook as a teacher of patience
969.howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Atisha's cook when teaching patience, alongside Shantideva's chapter on patience, and some practitioners deliberately treat difficult people as teachers in their daily mind training.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Atisha's Lamp, and the bird that can't fly before its wings grow. Your line: has the aim grown its wings.

Every kitchen has a temperature, and this one ran hot. When Atisha traveled to Tibet, the story goes, he brought along an attendant from India who cooked for him, and this man was difficult: rude, quick to snap, grumbling at everyone, his teacher included. The Tibetans who met him were puzzled. Why would a great master keep a man like that, when someone kinder could do the job? Atisha's answer, in the story, is still retold.
screen: `A HOT KITCHEN.` → `A RUDE ATTENDANT.` → `WHY KEEP HIM?`

segments.voice: In the legend, Atisha says the cook isn't a servant at all. He's a teacher, the one who teaches patience. Some tellings add a smile: the Tibetans were so gentle that, without the cook, Atisha would have had nothing left to practice on. It's told with a wink, but it lands on something serious. Shantideva's guide, the one we met two days ago, has a whole chapter on patience. There he argues that a person who harms you gives you something no friend can: the chance to practice patience. Without someone difficult, patience has nothing to grow on. He even compares an enemy to a treasure that turns up in your own house, unearned. Shantideva gives the argument; Atisha's cook puts it in a kitchen, with a face and a bad mood. It's one thing to agree that difficult people teach patience. It's another to keep one on the payroll. What it doesn't mean: the story isn't telling anyone to stay in harm's way or accept abuse. Buddhist teachers speak of patience alongside wisdom: seeing clearly what's happening, and refusing to add your own anger to it. The cook is grumpy, not dangerous. Closer to home, there may be a cook somewhere nearby: a coworker, a neighbor, a relative at the holiday table. The legend asks a quiet question. What if that person is the lesson, and not the obstacle to it?

970.title: Tilopa and Naropa
970.hook: the scholar Naropa leaves his university post to serve the wild teacher Tilopa
970.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, Tilopa and Naropa are honored at the head of the lineage, and the story of Naropa's search is told to students as a picture of devotion and of the gap between knowing words and knowing their meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Atisha's grumpy cook, kept on purpose. Your line: my teacher of patience.

Naropa had what scholars dream of. In the stories, he held a high post at Nalanda, a great monastic university in India, where he defended the teaching in debate and could recite texts by the shelf. One day, as he sat reading, a shadow fell across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the telling, asked him a question. Do you understand the words, or the meaning? Naropa said: the words. She laughed with delight. Then he added: and the meaning. And she wept.
screen: `A SCHOLAR AT NALANDA.` → `A SHADOW ON THE PAGE.` → `WORDS, OR MEANING?`

segments.voice: In Tibetan tellings, the old woman is a dakini, a wisdom figure in disguise. Her laughter and her tears say it all: Naropa knew the words, but not yet the meaning. When he asked who did, she named Tilopa. Naropa gave up his post and went looking, and the stories make it hard. He finds Tilopa nowhere and everywhere: in strange people on the road who disgust him, whom he refuses to help, and who turn out, too late, to have been Tilopa all along. When Naropa finally finds him, Tilopa looks nothing like a professor. In some tellings he's a wild man by a river, living on scraps of fish. He doesn't lecture. He sets Naropa trials, one after another, many of them painful and some frightening, and teaches through each one in a few words. The legend is extreme, and Kagyu tellings hold it up as a picture of devotion to a teacher. What it carries is a reversal: the celebrated scholar becomes the servant of someone with no titles, because that person knows the meaning. In the Kagyu tradition, Tilopa and Naropa stand at the head of a lineage, teacher to student, that we'll follow over the coming days. Knowing the words is good. Somewhere near you, someone with no credentials may know the meaning.

segments.voice: Let your mind move through people you'll meet today or met yesterday, the bus driver, a child, the person at the register, a neighbor you never talk to, and pause on one. Ask what this person might know that you don't, and let the question sit, unanswered, as you come back to the breath.
Dakini. A wisdom figure in disguise, like the old woman whose question sent Naropa to find his teacher Tilopa. Today's word.
Your line: the scholar served. Words first, and then the long road to their meaning. Until next time.

971.title: Marpa
971.hook: the farmer-translator who walked to India three times for the teachings
971.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school, Marpa is honored as the translator who brought Naropa's teachings to Tibet, and his image, often shown as a stocky layman rather than a monk, appears in Kagyu lineage paintings and prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dakini's question sent the scholar Naropa to find the wild teacher Tilopa. Your line: the scholar served.

He wasn't a monk. He had a wife, a farm, fields to watch and a temper to match, and he liked his beer, the stories say. And Tibetans remember him with deep honor. His name was Marpa, known as Marpa the Translator. Tradition says he made the trip from Tibet over the Himalaya to India three times, on foot, to find teachers and bring their words home.
screen: `NOT A MONK.` → `A FARMER WITH A TEMPER.` → `MARPA THE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: The teachings weren't free, and the road was dangerous: mountain passes, fevers in the hot plains below, robbers. In the stories, Marpa turned what he owned into gold to offer his teachers, and walked. In India he found Naropa, yesterday's scholar, now a master himself, and studied with him and others. He learned the language well enough to carry not only texts but their meaning, which yesterday's story says is the hard part. Each time, he came back to Tibet and worked: translating, teaching, farming. He didn't shave his head or enter a monastery. He showed that a householder could carry a lineage, with a family and a farm around him. Why go again? Tradition gives more than one reason: to fill gaps, to receive teachings he'd missed, to see his teacher once more. Marpa had enough to be a respected teacher at home, and still went back, because enough wasn't the point. The Kagyu tradition remembers him as the link between Naropa in India and the Tibetan students who came after. One of them, Milarepa, fills the next several days, and Marpa will turn out to be a fierce and strange teacher. His journeys leave a plain question: what would you walk a long way for? Not buy, not download. Walk for, come back with, and walk for again.

segments.voice: Ask quietly what is worth real effort to you, a skill, a relationship, a question, a practice, and let one thing come. Picture the first stretch of the road toward it, one small, concrete step, and see yourself taking it as the breath carries you on.
Marpa. The farmer and householder who, tradition says, walked to India three times and carried the teaching home as a translator. Today's word.
Your line: three journeys. Enough was never the point. Nine hundred seventy-one days, and counting.

972.title: Milarepa's remorse
972.hook: Milarepa used black magic to take revenge, then turned to the teaching in remorse
972.howItsDone: Milarepa's life story is read and retold in Tibetan Buddhist communities, and teachers use its opening, revenge and remorse, to show that even serious wrongdoing can be turned from through regret, purification and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marpa the farmer-translator, who walked to India and back for the teaching. Your line: three journeys.

A saint Tibetans hold dear begins his life story having caused many deaths. That isn't a rumor; it's how the story itself tells it. Milarepa was a boy when his father died. His uncle and aunt took charge of the family's fields and house, promising to hand them back when the boy grew up. They didn't. The widow and her children were left to work as servants on their own land, in rags. His mother never forgot it. And when Milarepa was grown, she put a demand to him that would change everything.
screen: `A FATHER DIES.` → `AN UNCLE TAKES THE FIELDS.` → `A MOTHER'S DEMAND.`

segments.voice: His mother sent him to learn black magic, and told him, in the story, that if he failed she would take her own life. He learned it. At the uncle's house, during a wedding feast, the building collapsed and many guests died, though the uncle and aunt survived. His mother rejoiced. When the villagers turned against her, he called down a hailstorm on their fields. Then the turn. The biography says he was filled with remorse: he couldn't sleep, couldn't eat, couldn't stop seeing what he had done. In Buddhist teaching, actions, karma, bring their results, and he knew that what he had set in motion would follow him. But his remorse didn't stop at guilt, which can just sit on a person. It got up and went looking. He sought out a teacher, then another, and finally heard the name Marpa, and the story says the name alone moved him to tears. Why start there? Tibetans could have told the life of a saint who was always good. Instead they keep the worst part in, at the start, in full. As teachers tell it, the message is plain: no one is too far gone to turn back. The harm is real, and the story never pretends otherwise. But the turn is real too. Milarepa will spend years paying for what he did.

segments.voice: Without digging for anything heavy, let one small harm you've been causing lately come to mind, a sharp tone, a habit, a word about someone behind their back, and name it plainly. If there's a sting, let it be there; then picture yourself turning, the way a person turns on a road, and setting that one harm down.
Milarepa's remorse. The sorrow over his revenge that didn't stop at guilt, but sent him looking for a teacher. Today's word.
Your line: he turned back. Remorse that went looking is where his road began. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

973.title: The towers
973.hook: Marpa has him build towers and tear them down, again and again
973.howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Milarepa's towers as a teaching on purifying past harm and on perseverance, and in the Kagyu tradition a tower in southern Tibet is honored as the one tradition says Milarepa finally completed for Marpa's son.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Milarepa's remorse, a sorrow that went looking for a teacher. Your line: he turned back.

Milarepa finally finds Marpa, the farmer-translator, plowing a field. He bows and asks for the teaching, offering himself, body, speech and mind. And Marpa, the teacher he has wept just to hear named, says something like this: fine, but you can't have food and teaching both. Choose. Milarepa has nothing to offer but his own two hands. So Marpa points to a ridge and gives him a job. Build me a tower.
screen: `MILAREPA FINDS MARPA.` → `FOOD OR TEACHING: CHOOSE.` → `BUILD ME A TOWER.`

segments.voice: Milarepa hauls stones on his back and builds the tower, alone. When it's partly done, Marpa comes to look and says he wasn't thinking clearly when he asked for it. Tear it down, and put every stone back where you found it. A new spot, a new shape, a new tower. Again Marpa changes his mind. Again it comes down. The story repeats it, and each time Milarepa's back grows more raw from the stones, and still no teaching comes. Marpa's wife, Dagmema, sees it all and pleads for him. She even helps him with a trick to win some teaching from another student, which Marpa later uncovers. Milarepa despairs and nearly gives up. Then, in the story, Marpa explains. The towers were never about towers. Milarepa had done terrible harm, and the endless labor, borne without anger, was a way to purify it. Marpa's harshness, he says, was itself the teaching. At last he accepts Milarepa as his student. The story is extreme, and it's about one student with one past; it's no rulebook for how a teacher may treat anyone. What it offers the rest of us is the rhythm: build, take it down, build again, without bitterness. And the week behind us: Shantideva's exchange of self and other. Atisha's lamp, and his cook for patience. Naropa serving Tilopa. Marpa walking to India and back. Milarepa turning from harm. And today, he picks up the first stone.
screen: `BUILD IT. TEAR IT DOWN.` · `AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` · `DAGMEMA PLEADS FOR HIM.` · `THE LABOR WAS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `BUILD IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Rest with the breath, and when your attention wanders off to a plan, a worry or a sound, don't scold it: set the stone down where you found it, and come back, like starting a new tower. Again, and again; each return is the practice, not a failure of it.
The towers. The ones Marpa had Milarepa build and tear down, again and again, as a way to purify his past. Today's word.
Your line: build it again. The labor, borne without anger, was the teaching. And that's the week.
